name: Anamorelin

lead: Anamorelin is an experimental oral drug that mimics ghrelin, the hunger hormone. Muscle-focused users follow it because it raised lean body mass in trials, pointing toward a fuller, more muscular physique.

It activates the ghrelin receptor in the brain and pituitary, increasing appetite and prompting growth hormone and IGF-1 release. Phase 3 trials in lung cancer patients (ROMANA 1 and 2) reported gains in lean body mass without clear gains in grip strength. It is approved in Japan for cachexia, and European regulators declined authorisation in 2017.

paras: It is a pill taken daily in cancer-cachexia trials and in Japan under prescription. It is discussed in appearance contexts as one of several ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues.
Safety data come from cancer-patient trials, and EU regulators cited inadequate safety recording. It is prescription-only and not marketed in most countries, and it is on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: Anamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor to raise appetite and growth hormone, which in trials increased lean body mass and points toward a fuller physique. Those trials were in cancer patients, and no trial has tested it for physique goals.

lead: Anamorelin is an investigational oral drug that activates the ghrelin receptor (also called the growth hormone secretagogue receptor). It has been developed for cancer cachexia, the wasting syndrome of appetite loss, weight loss and muscle loss seen in advanced cancer.[1][2] It also goes by the development codes ONO-7643 and RC-1291.[1]

Its clinical research is almost entirely in cancer patients. Phase 3 trials in non-small-cell lung cancer (ROMANA 1 and 2) reported gains in lean body mass but no clear improvement in handgrip strength, and the European Medicines Agency declined marketing authorisation in 2017.[1][3][4] A regulatory review reports that the drug was approved in Japan for cachexia in several cancer types.[5]

No published trial has tested anamorelin for cosmetic, bodybuilding or aesthetic purposes. It is discussed in appearance-related contexts mainly as one of several ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues. It is listed among substances prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1]
infobox: Approved in Japan for cancer cachexia; EU authorisation refused in 2017[1][5]

paras: The main studied indication is cancer anorexia-cachexia, which is common in advanced cancer and is associated with reduced food intake, loss of lean mass and reduced function.[2][6] Cachexia prevalence is estimated at 50-80% in advanced cancer.[2]
In Japan the drug was reported to be approved for cachexia in non-small-cell lung, gastric, pancreatic and colorectal cancer.[5] It has not been authorised in the European Union.[1]

Anamorelin is a non-peptide, centrally penetrant agonist of the ghrelin receptor. Activating the receptor increases appetite and stimulates release of growth hormone, which raises insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels.[1][4] Researchers describe it as an oral ghrelin mimetic with both appetite-enhancing and anabolic effects.[4][7]
Its elimination half-life is reported as roughly 6-7 hours, which allows once-daily oral dosing in trials.[1]

A pooled analysis of two phase 2 trials in patients with cancer anorexia-cachexia assessed body composition, strength, quality of life and safety.[4] Phase 3 results followed in ROMANA 1 and 2, two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials at 93 sites in 19 countries.[3]

Wikipedia summarises the EMA assessment as finding only a marginal effect on lean body mass, no proven effect on handgrip strength or quality of life, and incomplete safety data recording, leading to a conclusion that risks outweighed benefits.[1] Japanese trials in lung cancer and gastrointestinal cancer patients reported on efficacy and safety within that population.[8][9][10]

The ROMANA 3 extension study was designed as a long-term safety follow-up of patients from the phase 3 trials.[11] Safety was a point of contention in the EU review, where the regulator cited inadequate recording of safety data.[1]

Phase 2 results were published in 2013 and 2015, and the ROMANA phase 3 trials reported in 2016.[1][4][3][4] In May 2017 the EMA recommended refusing marketing authorisation, and confirmed the refusal in September 2017 after re-examination.[1] The Japanese regulatory review of the drug was published in 2021.[5]

Human trials include phase 2 studies in non-small-cell lung cancer, the phase 3 ROMANA 1, 2 and 3 programme, Japanese phase 2 and 3 studies and a single-arm study in advanced gastrointestinal cancer.[3][4][8][9][10][11][12][13][14] A phase 1 study registered a ghrelin receptor agonist for effects on muscle and bone in people with sarcopenia and osteopenia.[15] A later US-registered phase 3 programme in lung cancer completed enrolment, and a phase 2 trial in pancreatic cancer was terminated early with four participants.[16][17][18]
All of these studies are in disease populations. No studies in healthy people or for appearance outcomes were found.

Anamorelin appears on the WADA prohibited list among ghrelin-receptor agonists and growth hormone secretagogues.[1] It is not an over-the-counter product, and it has not been marketed in the EU or US.[1]
